title: Microexpressions (The Brief Truth Leak)
description: Fleeting facial expressions—lasting less than half a second—that reveal concealed emotions. When someone tries to hide anger, fear, or disgust, the true feeling often flashes before the mask is put on.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Fleeting facial expressions—lasting less than half a second—that reveal concealed emotions. When someone tries to hide anger, fear, or disgust, the true feeling often flashes before the mask is put on.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A person says “I’m happy for you” and a micro‑expression of contempt (one‑sided lip raise) flits across their face.
During a serious denial, a tiny smile (duper’s delight) appears and vanishes.
Someone claims not to be worried, but their eyebrows briefly pull together in fear before relaxing.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: The expression is incongruent with the words.
It’s so fast you might miss it, but you feel “something was off.”
The person quickly neutralizes the face after the leak.

sections.title: Real Phrases
sections.content: (No phrases; this is nonverbal, but you might sense the mismatch.)

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: A flash of disgust when discussing someone they claim to love.
A micro‑shrug (brief shoulder lift) accompanying a denial.
A split‑second tightening of the jaw when a name is mentioned.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Paul Ekman’s research showed that some emotional expressions are universal and involuntary. The brain’s initial emotional response can’t always be suppressed fast enough, leading to a micro‑expression leak.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Do not rely on microexpressions alone. They are rare, easy to miss, and hard to interpret. Use them as a prompt to ask more questions.
If you see an incongruent flash, note it and probe the topic further without accusing.
Training with tools (METT) can improve recognition, but it’s not a superpower.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming any fleeting expression is a lie indicator. Sometimes it’s just a random facial twitch.
Over‑diagnosing “duper’s delight” when someone is just nervously smiling.
Believing that reading microexpressions makes you a human lie detector. It’s one piece of the puzzle.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A politician is asked if he supports a colleague. He says “Absolutely,” but for a fraction of a second, his nose wrinkles and lip rises in disgust. The clip goes viral, and analysts note the micro‑expression as the real feeling. He later withdraws support.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The face is a quick truth‑teller. Before the brain edits the response, the emotion has already RSVP’d.
